==Problem 7==
Janet rolls a standard <imath>6</imath>-sided die <imath>4</imath> times and keeps a running total of the numbers she rolls. What is the probability that at some point, her running total will equal <imath>3</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }\frac{2}{9}\qquad\textbf{(B) }\frac{49}{216}\qquad\textbf{(C) }\frac{25}{108}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\frac{17}{72}\qquad\textbf{(E) }\frac{13}{54}</imath>

==Solution 1 (Casework)==

There are <imath>3</imath> cases where the running total will equal <imath>3</imath>: one roll; two rolls; or three rolls:

'''Case 1:'''
The chance of rolling a running total of <imath>3</imath>, namely <imath>(3)</imath> in exactly one roll is <imath>\frac{1}{6}</imath>.

'''Case 2:'''
The chance of rolling a running total of <imath>3</imath> in exactly two rolls, namely <imath>(1, 2)</imath> and <imath>(2, 1)</imath> is <imath>\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{6}\cdot2=\frac{1}{18}</imath>.

'''Case 3:'''
The chance of rolling a running total of 3 in exactly three rolls, namely <imath>(1, 1, 1)</imath> is <imath>\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{216}</imath>.

Using the rule of sum we have <imath>\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{18}+\frac{1}{216}=\boxed{\textbf{(B) }\frac{49}{216}}</imath>.

~walmartbrian ~andyluo ~DRBStudent ~MC_ADe

==Solution 2 (Brute Force)==

Because there is only a maximum of 3 rolls we must count (running total = 3 means there can't be a fourth roll counted), we can simply list out all of the probabilities.

If we roll a 1 on the first, the rolls that follow must be 2 or {1,1}, with the following results not mattering. This leaves a probability of <imath>\frac{1}{6}\times\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6}\times\frac{1}{6}\times\frac{1}{6} = \frac{7}{216}</imath>.

If we roll a 2 on the first, the roll that follows must be 1, resulting in a probability of <imath>\frac{1}{6}\times\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}</imath>.

If we roll a 3 on the first, the following rolls do not matter, resulting in a probability of <imath>\frac{1}{6}</imath>.
Any roll greater than three will result in a running total greater than 3 no matter what, so those cases can be ignored.
Summing the answers, we have <imath>\frac{7}{216} + \frac{1}{36} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{7+6+36}{216} = \boxed{\textbf{(B) }\frac{49}{216}}</imath>.

~Failure.net

==Solution 3==

Consider sequences of 4 integers with each integer between 1 and 6, the number of permutations of 6 numbers is <imath>6^4=1296</imath>. 

The following 4 types of sequences that might generate a running total of the numbers to be equal to 3 (x, y, or z denotes any integer between 1 and 6).

Sequence #1, (1, 1, 1, x): there are <imath>6</imath> possible sequences. 

Sequence #2, (1, 2, x, y): there are <imath>6^2 = 36</imath> possible sequences. 

Sequence #3, (2, 1, x, y): there are <imath>6^2 = 36</imath> possible sequences. 

Sequence #4, (3, x, y, z): there are <imath>6^3 = 216</imath> possible sequences.

Out of 1296 possible sequences, there are a total of <imath>6 + 36 + 36 + 216 = 294</imath> sequences that qualify. Hence, the probability is <imath>294 / 1296 = \boxed{\textbf{(B) }\frac{49}{216}}</imath>

~sqroot

==Solution 4 (cheese-ish)==

You have to add 1/216 for the case 1-1-1, so it should have denominator 216. Therefore, the answer is B: 49/216

-Supernova77
